pieces: Salut
" is the casual hello you use with friends and family; "Bonjour" is the polite one.
Bonjour
" is the polite hello you use with strangers, in shops or at work; "Salut" is only for friends.
Bonsoir
" is the greeting for the evening. "Bonjour" is used during the day.
Au revoir
" is the standard way to say goodbye in any situation; "Bonjour" is hello, not goodbye.
À bientôt
" means "see you soon": "bientôt" means "soon", and you say it when you expect to meet again before long.
Bonjour, madame, je m'appelle Paul.
" is a polite greeting followed by an introduction: "je m'appelle" means "my name is".
Bonsoir, à bientôt et merci.
" strings together three useful phrases: "bonsoir" is the evening hello, "à bientôt" means see you soon, and "merci" means thank you.
Bonjour, merci beaucoup.
" combines the polite hello "Bonjour" with "merci beaucoup", meaning "thank you very much".
S'il vous plaît
" is the polite way to say please; with a friend you say "s'il te plaît".
Merci
" is the standard way to say "thank you" in French, and it works with anyone.
De rien
" literally means "it's nothing" and is the everyday reply when someone says "merci".
Excusez-moi
" is the polite "excuse me" for getting a stranger's attention. It uses the vous form.
Désolé
" means "sorry" and is used to apologise. A woman writes it "Désolée".
Excusez-moi, je suis désolé.
" ends with "désolé" (sorry), a different word from "malade", "fatigué" or "content", so listen for the last word.
Parlez lentement, s'il vous plaît.
" uses "parlez", the vous command form of parler, with "lentement" (slowly); "s'il vous plaît" keeps the request polite for a stranger.
Oui
" is the French word for "yes". The other options are greetings or welcomes, not answers to a question.
Non
" is the French word for "no", the opposite of "oui".
Comment allez-vous ?
" is the polite way to ask how someone is; "Comment vous appelez-vous ?" asks their name instead.
Je vais bien, merci
" literally means "I am going well, thanks". French uses the verb aller (to go) to say how you are.
Comment vous appelez-vous ?
" is the polite way to ask someone's name (literally "how do you call yourself?"); "Je m'appelle..." is the reply.
The speaker says "
Je m'appelle Marie, enchantée.
", which means "My name is Marie, nice to meet you." The other choices change one word to something that sounds clearly different.
Parlez-vous anglais, s'il vous plaît ?
" is a polite way to ask a stranger whether they speak English; vous is used with people you don't know.
Excusez-moi
" is the polite vous form you say to a stranger when you need to get past them; "
Pardon
" works too.
Je m'appelle...
" means "my name is..." (literally "I call myself"); you follow it with your name.
Enchanté
" is what you say when you meet someone for the first time; a woman writes "Enchantée", which sounds the same.
Bonne nuit
" is said at bedtime or late at night when parting; "Au revoir" is just a general goodbye.
À demain
" means "see you tomorrow" because "demain" means "tomorrow".
Bienvenue
" is what you say to greet someone arriving, like "welcome" in English.
The sentence "
Bonsoir, je m'appelle Marie.
" greets someone in the evening with "Bonsoir" and then gives a name with "je m'appelle".
Désolé.
" is the simple way to say you are sorry; a woman writes "Désolée", which sounds the same.
Bien sûr
" means "of course"; you use it to say yes or to agree warmly.
Je ne comprends pas
" is the negative of "je comprends" (I understand): French wraps the verb in ne ... pas to say "not".
Pouvez-vous répéter, s'il vous plaît ?
" politely asks someone to say something again: "répéter" means "to repeat" and "pouvez-vous" means "can you".
Parlez-vous anglais ?
" is a polite question made by putting the verb before "vous"; "anglais" means "English".
Bonne chance
" means "good luck"; "chance" is feminine, so the adjective is "bonne", not "bon".
The speaker says "
Je ne comprends pas, désolé.
", meaning "I don't understand, sorry." The other choices change one clearly audible word.
Excusez-moi, je ne comprends pas
" means "Excuse me, I don't understand." "Ne … pas" wraps around the verb "comprends" to make it negative.
Parlez-vous français ?
" is the polite question for "Do you speak French?", with the verb placed before "vous" and "français" meaning "French".
un
" is the French number 1; it is also the word for "a" before a masculine noun, as in un café.
deux
" is the French word for 2; the final x is silent when the word stands alone.
trois
" is the French word for 3; the final s is silent, so it sounds like "trwah".
quatre
" is the French word for 4; it starts with qu-, which sounds like a k.
cinq
" is the French word for 5; note the unusual -nq spelling at the end.

spans: J'ai trois frères et deux sœurs.
pieces: J'ai trois frères et deux sœurs.
" means 'I have three brothers and two sisters'; the numbers trois and deux are the words to listen for.
J'ai cinq euros.
" uses j'ai ('I have') followed by the number cinq and the noun euros.
six
" is the French word for 6; it looks like the English word, but on its own it is pronounced "seess", with a clear s sound at the end.
sept
" is the French word for 7; the p is silent, so it sounds like "set".
huit
" is the French word for 8; the h is silent and it sounds like "weet".
neuf
" means nine (9); don't mix it up with "cinq" (5) or "treize" (13).
dix
" means ten (10); it is the base for 17, 18 and 19 ("dix-sept", "dix-huit", "dix-neuf").
The speaker says "
J'ai huit ans.
", meaning I am eight years old; huit sounds like "weet" and is clearly different from dix, neuf and sept.
Il y a dix euros
" means there are ten euros; before the vowel of euros, the x of dix links as a z sound, so you say "di-zeuro".
J'ai neuf euros.
" uses j'ai (I have) followed by neuf, the word for nine.
onze
" means eleven (11); it is the first of the special words for 11 to 16, so it is not built from "dix".
douze
" means twelve (12); it comes right after "onze" (11).
treize
" means thirteen (13); like the other numbers from 11 to 16, it ends in -ze.
quatorze
" means fourteen (14); it comes from "quatre" (4), like fourteen comes from four.
quinze
" means fifteen (15); "quatorze" is 14, so don't mix them up.
The speaker says "
J'ai quinze euros.
", which means I have fifteen euros; quinze is 15, so don't mix it up with treize, douze or onze.
J'ai quatorze euros.
" uses j'ai (I have) with quatorze, the French word for fourteen (14).
seize
" means sixteen (16); it is the last special word before French counts "dix-sept" (ten-seven).
dix-sept
" means seventeen: ten ("dix") plus seven ("sept"), joined with a hyphen.
dix-huit
" means eighteen: ten ("dix") plus eight ("huit"), joined with a hyphen.
dix-neuf
" is built as dix (ten) + neuf (nine), joined with a hyphen, just like "dix-huit" (eighteen).
vingt
" means twenty. Its final -gt is silent, so it sounds like "vin".
The speaker says "
J'ai dix-sept ans.
" (I am seventeen years old); dix-sept sounds different from dix-huit, seize and vingt.
J'ai douze euros
" means I have twelve euros; douze is a single word, and "J'ai" is je plus ai, written with an apostrophe.
The number after sixteen is seventeen, written "
dix-sept
": ten ("dix") plus seven ("sept"), joined with a hyphen.
vingt et un
" means twenty-one; 21, 31, 41 and so on use "et" (and), unlike "vingt-deux" (22).
trente
" means thirty (30); it is the tens word that comes after "vingt" (20).
quarante
" means forty; don't mix it up with "quatre" (four) or "cent" (one hundred).
cinquante
" means fifty; it starts like "cinq" (five), just as fifty starts like five.
cent
" means one hundred; French just says "
cent
", not "un cent".
The speaker says "
J'ai quarante ans.
", meaning 'I am forty years old'; French uses avoir (to have) for age, and "quarante" is forty.
J'ai cinquante euros.
" Use "j'ai" (I have) plus the number and the noun; "euros" follows the number directly, with no "de".
la mère
" means mother; "la" shows it is a feminine noun, unlike "le fils" (son) or "le voisin" (neighbour).
le père
" means father; its partner word is "la mère" (mother).
la sœur
" means sister. It is feminine, so it takes "la", and it is spelled with the joined letters œ.
le frère
" means brother, a male sibling; don't confuse it with "la sœur" (sister) or "le cousin" (cousin).
le fils
" means son; the final s is pronounced ("feess"). "l'enfant" means any child, not specifically a son.
The speaker says "
Mon père est ici.
", meaning my father is here. The wrong choices change one word you can hear: mère, frère or là-bas.

spans: Voici ma sœur et mon frère
pieces: Voici ma sœur et mon frère
" means here are my sister and my brother. Use "ma" with the feminine sœur and "mon" with the masculine frère.
Ma mère a un fils.
" uses "a" (has) from avoir, "ma" for the feminine mère, and "un fils" for a son.
la fille
" means daughter (it also means girl). "le fils" is the son and "la sœur" is the sister.
la grand-mère
" means grandmother: grand + mère (mother), joined with a hyphen.
le grand-père
" means grandfather: grand + père (father). "la grand-mère" is the grandmother.
la tante
" means aunt, the sister of your mother or father.
l'oncle
" means uncle. The word is masculine (un oncle), and le becomes l' before the vowel.

spans: Ma tante est la sœur de mon père.
pieces: The sentence is "
Ma tante est la sœur de mon père.
" and it means 'My aunt is my father's sister.' The other choices change one word: fille, femme or frère.

spans: Ma grand-mère est une amie de ma tante.
pieces: Ma grand-mère est une amie de ma tante.
" uses ma before the feminine words grand-mère and tante, and une amie because the friend is a woman. De links the friend to the person she is a friend of.
le cousin
" is a male cousin; the masculine form ends in -in, pronounced nasally.
la cousine
" is a female cousin: add -e to le cousin and pronounce the n. "le cousin" is the male form.
le mari
" means husband. For wife, French usually says la femme.
l'épouse
" means wife; in everyday speech French more often says "ma femme" (my wife).
l'ami
" is a male friend; a female friend is "l'amie", with an extra -e.
The sentence is "
Mon cousin est très gentil.
" and it means 'My cousin is very nice.' Voisin rhymes with cousin, so listen for the first sound: cousin starts with a k sound.
Mon ami est mon voisin.
" means "My friend is my neighbor." Use mon before ami and voisin, since both are masculine words for a male friend and a male neighbor.

spans: Mon mari est l'ami de mon cousin.
pieces: Mon mari est l'ami de mon cousin.
" uses mari for husband and ami for a male friend, joined by de to show whose friend he is.
l'amie
" is a female friend; the extra -e marks the feminine (a male friend is "l'ami").
l'homme
" means man; the h is silent, so le becomes l'.
la femme
" means woman (and also wife); it is pronounced "fam".
l'enfant
" means child, a boy or a girl; le or la becomes l' before the vowel.
le bébé
" means "baby". The noun is masculine, so it takes "le" even when the baby is a girl.

spans: Mon ami habite avec sa mère.
pieces: The speaker says "
Mon ami habite avec sa mère.
", meaning my friend lives with his mother; "mère" (mother) sounds clearly different from père, tante and frère.
Mon amie a un bébé.
" uses "amie" for a female friend, "a" for has, and "bébé", which is masculine and takes "un".
le garçon
" means "boy". Its counterpart for a girl is "la fille".
le voisin
" means "neighbour", the person who lives next door. A female neighbour is "la voisine".
le collègue
" means "colleague", someone you work with. Note the accent on the first e, and that a woman is "la collègue".
le professeur
" means "teacher", especially in secondary school. In everyday speech people often shorten it to "le prof".
l'étudiant
" means a (male) student; a female student is "l'étudiante".
The sentence "
Le voisin est mon ami.
" means "The neighbour is my friend." The wrong choices change one clearly different word: garçon, oncle or collègue.
Mon voisin est étudiant
" means 'My neighbor is a student.' French leaves out the article after être when you give someone's job or status, so you say "est étudiant", not "est un étudiant".
Mon collègue est étudiant.
" says your colleague is a student. After être, French usually drops the article before a profession or status like étudiant.
rouge
" means "red". It already ends in -e, so it stays the same for masculine and feminine nouns.
bleu
" means blue; "gris", "vert" and "violet" mean grey, green and purple.
vert
" means green; "noir", "rouge" and "rose" mean black, red and pink.
jaune
" means yellow; "rouge", "noir" and "marron" mean red, black and brown.
noir
" means black; "violet" is purple, "bleu" is blue and "gris" is grey.
The sentence heard is "
Elle porte une robe rouge.
", meaning she is wearing a red dress. The other choices change only the colour.
The adjective agrees with the feminine noun, so "
La voiture est verte.
" uses "verte"; you can also say "de couleur verte" or use "
C'est une voiture verte.
blanc
" means white; "noir" is black, "bleu" is blue and "rose" is pink.
gris
" means grey; "marron" is brown, "jaune" is yellow and "rouge" is red.
marron
" means brown, and it never changes its ending (des chaussures marron); "gris" is grey, "vert" is green and "blanc" is white.
rose
" means pink; "bleu" is blue, "noir" is black and "violet" is purple.
violet
" means purple; "rouge" is red, "jaune" is yellow and "marron" is brown.
The speaker says "
Elle porte une robe rose.
" meaning she is wearing a pink dress; the other choices name different colours.
Il porte un pull gris
" means 'He is wearing a grey sweater', using the colour gris after the clothing word.
Il porte une chemise blanche.
" uses porter for wearing, and blanche is feminine to agree with chemise.
la chemise
" means a shirt; "la robe" is a dress, "les gants" are gloves and "la veste" is a jacket.
t-shirt →
le t-shirt
. Common colours and clothing items.
le pantalon
" means trousers, and it is singular in French although "trousers" is plural in English; "la jupe" is a skirt, "le pull" a sweater and "la chemise" a shirt.
la robe
" means a dress; "les bottes" are boots, "le manteau" is a coat and "la jupe" is a skirt.
la jupe
" means a skirt; "les bottes" are boots, "le manteau" is a coat and "les chaussettes" are socks.
The sentence "
Elle porte une jupe rouge.
" means she is wearing a red skirt; the other choices change the clothing or the colour.
Il porte une chemise bleue.
" uses porter for wearing, and the adjective bleue agrees with the feminine noun la chemise.
les chaussures
" means shoes; "la veste" is a jacket, "les gants" are gloves and "le pantalon" is trousers.
A jacket is "
la veste
"; it is feminine, so it takes "la". Don't confuse it with "le manteau", which is a longer, warmer coat.
A coat is "
le manteau
"; it is masculine, so it takes "le". A lighter jacket would be "la veste".
A hat is "
le chapeau
"; it is masculine, and its plural adds -x: "les chapeaux".
A scarf is "
l'écharpe
"; the word is feminine, but "la" shortens to "l'" before the vowel "é".

spans: Elle porte une robe rouge aujourd'hui.
pieces: The speaker says "
Elle porte une robe rouge aujourd'hui.
" meaning she is wearing a red dress today; the other choices change the colour, the clothing or the day.
Il porte un manteau noir
" means he is wearing a black coat; "manteau" is masculine, so it takes "un" and the colour stays in the masculine form.

spans: La femme porte une jupe bleue.
pieces: La femme porte une jupe bleue.
" uses "porte" for wearing, and "bleue" takes an -e because "jupe" is feminine.
Socks are "
les chaussettes
"; don't confuse them with "les chaussures", which are shoes.
A sweater is "
le pull
", short for "le pull-over"; it is masculine, so it takes "le".
A belt is "
la ceinture
"; it is feminine, so it takes "la".
Gloves are "
les gants
"; they come in pairs, so the word is plural with "les" (one glove is "un gant").
Boots are "
les bottes
"; the word is plural, so it takes "les" (one boot is "une botte").
The sentence is "
Elle porte une robe bleue.
" and means 'She is wearing a blue dress.'; "robe" (dress) and "bleue" (blue) are the words to listen for.
Il porte un pull bleu.
" uses porter for wearing; the adjective bleu comes after the masculine noun pull.
lundi
" means "Monday", the first day of the French week. Days of the week take no capital letter in French.
mardi
" means "Tuesday", the day after "lundi". It is written with a small letter in French.
mercredi
" means "Wednesday", the middle of the week. It is written with a small letter in French.
jeudi
" means "Thursday", the day after "mercredi". It is written with a small letter in French.
Friday is "
vendredi
", the day after "jeudi" (Thursday). French day names are written in lowercase.
The sentence "
Aujourd'hui, c'est lundi.
" means "Today is Monday." The other choices name different days: mardi, jeudi and samedi.
Aujourd'hui, c'est vendredi
" means "Today is Friday." French uses "c'est" plus the day name to say which day it is, and the day name stays in lowercase.
Aujourd'hui, c'est mercredi.
" is the usual way to say that today is Wednesday. In French the day name takes no capital letter.
Saturday is "
samedi
"; don't confuse it with "dimanche", which is Sunday, the day after.
Sunday is "
dimanche
"; it is the only day of the week that does not end in -di.
janvier
" means January. Unlike in English, French month names start with a lowercase letter.
février
" means February. Note the accent on the first e (é) and the lowercase f.
mars
" means March. It looks like the English word, but it is not capitalised and the final s is pronounced.

spans: Aujourd'hui, c'est lundi et il pleut.
pieces: The speaker says "
Aujourd'hui, c'est lundi et il pleut.
", meaning today is Monday and it is raining; "lundi" (Monday) and "pleut" (rains) are the key words to listen for.
Mon anniversaire est en mars.
" uses en before a month name to mean in, and the month stays lowercase in French.
avril
" means April. It is close to the English word, with a v instead of the p, and it is written in lowercase.
mai
" means May. It sounds much like the English word and, like all French months, it is written in lowercase.
juin
" means June. Don't confuse it with "juillet" (July), which is the longer word.
juillet
" means July. The double l and the -et ending set it apart from "juin" (June).
août
" means August. Remember the circumflex on the u; the word is pronounced like "oo" or "oot".
The sentence "
Mon anniversaire est en juin.
" means 'My birthday is in June.' The months juin, mai, août and avril all sound clearly different.
Nous sommes en août
" means 'It is August' (literally 'We are in August'). Use "en" before a month in French.
Mon anniversaire est en juin.
" uses "en" before a month to mean "in", and the month stays in lowercase.
septembre
" means September. It is like the English word, but it ends in -bre and is written in lowercase.
octobre
" means "October". Like all French months, it is written with a small letter.
novembre
" means "November", the month after "octobre". French months are written with a small letter.
December is "
décembre
". In French, month names take no capital letter, and note the accent on the é.
Spring is "
le printemps
". It is the only season that keeps "le", because it starts with a consonant; you say "au printemps" for "in spring".
The sentence "
Mon anniversaire est en décembre.
" means 'My birthday is in December.' Listen to the start of the month: "décembre" begins with dé-, while "novembre" begins with no-.
J'aime le printemps.
" uses "j'aime" (I like) followed by "le printemps" (spring). In French you keep "le" when you speak about a season in general.
Summer is "
l'été
". "Le" shortens to "l'" before a vowel, and "in summer" is "en été".
Autumn is "
l'automne
". The "m" is silent, so it sounds like "o-tonn", and "in autumn" is "en automne".
Winter is "
l'hiver
". The h is silent, so "le" shortens to "l'", and "in winter" is "en hiver".
Today is "
aujourd'hui
". Don't confuse it with "maintenant" (now) or "ce soir" (tonight).
Tomorrow is "
demain
". Its opposite is "hier" (yesterday).
The sentence "
Nous sommes en hiver aujourd'hui.
" means we are in winter today; the other choices change the season or swap "aujourd'hui" for "demain".
Demain, c'est lundi
" means tomorrow is Monday, using "demain" for tomorrow and a day of the week.
C'est l'été maintenant.
" uses "l'été" for summer and "maintenant" for now; "nous sommes en été" is another natural way to say it.
Head is "
la tête
". It is feminine, so it takes "la", and the ê has a circumflex.
Hair on your head is "
les cheveux
". It is plural in French, unlike English; "un cheveu" is a single hair.
Eye is "
l'œil
". Its plural is completely different: "les yeux" (eyes).
les yeux
" means eyes. It is the irregular plural of "l'œil" (eye).
l'oreille
" means ear. It is a feminine noun, and le/la becomes l' before a vowel sound.
J'ai mal à la tête.
" means I have a headache; "la tête" (head) sounds clearly different from "la main" (hand), "la dent" (tooth) and "la bouche" (mouth).
Mes cheveux sont longs.
" works because "les cheveux" is plural in French, so the verb is "sont" and the adjective takes the plural "longs".
le nez
" means nose. It is masculine, and the final z is silent.
la bouche
" means "mouth". It is a feminine noun, so it takes la, as in « Ouvre la bouche » (Open your mouth).
la dent
" means "tooth". It is feminine, and the plural is les dents, as in « se brosser les dents » (to brush your teeth).
le cou
" means "neck". It is masculine, so it takes le; don't confuse it with le coude (elbow).
l'épaule
" means "shoulder". It is feminine (une épaule), and la becomes l' before the vowel sound é.
Elle ouvre la bouche.
" means "She opens her mouth". Listen for the noun at the end: bouche (mouth) sounds clearly different from porte (door), main (hand) or fenêtre (window).
Ouvre la bouche
" means Open your mouth; la bouche is feminine, so it takes la.
J'ai mal au cou.
" uses avoir mal à plus the body part; à + le becomes au before le cou.
le bras
" means "arm". It is masculine, the final s is silent, and the plural is the same: les bras.
la main
" means "hand". It is feminine even though it ends in a consonant, so it takes la.
le doigt
" means "finger". It is masculine, and the g and t are silent, so it sounds like "dwa".
la poitrine
" means "chest". It is a feminine noun, so it takes la.
le dos
" means "back" (the body part). It is masculine, and the final s is silent.
J'ai mal au bras.
" means "My arm hurts". The other choices name different body parts: back, finger and stomach.
To say a body part hurts, French uses "
J'ai mal à la main.
" (literally 'I have pain at the hand'); "la main" is feminine, so it takes à la.
le ventre
" means "stomach" or "belly", as in « J'ai mal au ventre » (I have a stomach ache). It is masculine, so it takes le.
la jambe
" means "leg". It is feminine, so it takes la; don't confuse it with le pied (foot).
Knee is "
le genou
". It is masculine, and its plural ends in x: "les genoux".
Foot is "
le pied
". The d is silent, and "on foot" is "à pied".
"Skin" is "
la peau
", a feminine noun. Don't confuse it with "la poitrine", which means chest.
The speaker says "
J'ai mal au ventre aujourd'hui.
" meaning they have a stomach ache today; the other choices name a knee, a foot or an arm.
J'ai mal à la jambe
" means "My leg hurts." La jambe is feminine, so the French uses à la before it.
J'ai mal au pied.
" is the usual way to say your foot hurts; le pied is masculine, so à + le becomes au.
"Face" is "
le visage
". It is masculine even though it ends in -e.
"Heart" is "
le cœur
", a masculine noun spelled with the joined letters œ.
"Elbow" is "
le coude
". "Le bras" is the whole arm, not the joint in the middle.
"Wrist" is "
le poignet
", a masculine noun. The final t is silent.
"Chin" is "
le menton
". "Le nez" is the nose, just above it.
J'ai mal au dos.
" means "My back hurts." The pattern is "avoir mal à" plus a body part, and "à + le" becomes "au" with masculine "dos".
J'ai mal au menton.
" uses "avoir mal à" plus the body part, and "à + le" becomes "au" before the masculine noun "menton".
"House" is "
la maison
", a feminine noun, so you say une maison.
"Apartment" is "
l'appartement
". The article becomes l' before a vowel. The word is masculine (un appartement) and is spelled with a double p.
la cuisine
" means "kitchen", the room where you cook. It is feminine, and the same word also means cooking or cuisine.
la chambre
" is the room where you sleep, so it means "bedroom". Don't confuse it with "la salle à manger", the dining room.
la salle de bain
" literally means "room of bath", the room where you wash, so it is the "bathroom".
J'habite dans une petite maison.
" means "I live in a small house." The key words are "petite" (small) and "maison" (house).

spans: Ma chambre est à côté de la cuisine
pieces: Ma chambre est à côté de la cuisine
" means "My bedroom is next to the kitchen." The phrase "à côté de" tells you where one room is in relation to another.
J'habite dans un appartement.
" means "I live in an apartment." The word appartement is masculine, so it takes un.
le salon
" is the room where you sit, relax and welcome guests, so it means "living room".
la salle à manger
" literally means "room for eating" (manger = to eat), so it is the "dining room".
le jardin
" is the outdoor area with grass, flowers or vegetables next to a house, so it means "garden".
la porte
" is what you open and close to go into a room or a house, so it means "door".
la fenêtre
" is the glass opening in a wall that lets light in, so it means "window".
The sentence is "
Nous avons un grand jardin.
" and means "We have a big garden." The other choices change the noun to a different room or object.

spans: Le salon est à côté de la cuisine.
pieces: Le salon est à côté de la cuisine.
" uses "à côté de" to mean "next to"; "près de" (near) is also a natural way to say it.
le mur
" is each vertical side of a room or building, so it means "wall".
le sol
" is the surface you walk on inside a room, so it means "floor". "le toit" is the roof and "le tapis" is a rug.
le plafond
" is the top surface of a room, above your head, so it means "ceiling".
l'escalier
" is the set of steps leading to another floor; French uses the singular where English says "stairs".
"Roof" is "
le toit
", a masculine noun. The final t is silent.

spans: La table est dans la cuisine.
pieces: The speaker says "
La table est dans la cuisine.
", meaning the table is in the kitchen; the other choices change the object (chaise, lampe) or the room (chambre).

spans: Le mur de la cuisine est blanc.
pieces: In "
Le mur de la cuisine est blanc.
" you describe a wall with a color: "est" links the noun to the adjective, and "blanc" is masculine because "le mur" is masculine.

spans: Ma maison a une grande cuisine.
pieces: Ma maison a une grande cuisine.
" uses avoir to say what the house has; "grande" goes before the feminine noun "cuisine".
"Garage" is "
le garage
", a masculine noun. Careful: "la gare" means train station.
"Table" is "
la table
", a feminine noun. "Le tableau" looks similar but means a painting or a board.
"Chair" is "
la chaise
", a feminine noun. Don't mix it up with "la porte", the door.
le lit
" means bed, the piece of furniture you sleep in. Lit is masculine, so it takes "le". Don't confuse it with la chambre, the bedroom.
le canapé
" means sofa (couch). Canapé is masculine, so it takes "le".
The sentence is "
J'habite dans une grande maison.
", meaning I live in a big house. The other choices change only the final noun, which sounds clearly different.

spans: J'habite dans une maison avec un jardin.
pieces: J'habite dans une maison avec un jardin.
" uses "habiter" to say where you live, and "avec" means 'with'. "Maison" is feminine so it takes "une", while "jardin" is masculine so it takes "un".
la lampe
" means lamp, and it looks almost like the English word. Lampe is feminine, so it takes "la".
le miroir
" means mirror, the glass you look at yourself in. Miroir is masculine, so it takes "le".
la clé
" means key, the thing that opens a door. Clé is feminine, so it takes "la".
l'étagère
" means shelf. Étagère is a feminine noun starting with a vowel, so la becomes l'.
le tapis
" is the piece of fabric laid on the floor, so it means "carpet" or rug. "le sol" is the floor itself.
J'habite dans un petit appartement.
" means I live in a small apartment. The other choices change one word: garage, studio or grand (big).

spans: La clé est sur la table.
pieces: La clé est sur la table.
" means The key is on the table. Clé is feminine, so it takes "la".
Ma cuisine est petite.
" means My kitchen is small. Cuisine is feminine, so the adjective takes the feminine form petite.
manger
" means to eat. It is a regular -er verb, as in Je mange une pomme.
boire
" means "to drink", as in "boire de l'eau" (to drink water). It is an irregular verb, so learn it by heart.
parler
" means "to speak", as in "parler français". It is a regular -er verb.
écouter
" means "to listen", as in "écouter de la musique". Don't confuse it with "regarder", which means "to watch".
lire
" means "to read", as in "lire un livre". "Regarder" means "to watch", not "to read".
Je veux boire de l'eau.
" means "I want to drink water"; listen for the verb boire (to drink) and the drink, de l'eau (water).
To say you want to do something, use vouloir followed by the infinitive, as in "
Je veux boire de l'eau.
" "Je voudrais" (vouloir) and "J'aimerais" (aimer) are politer ways to say the same thing.
écrire
" means "to write", as in "écrire une lettre". Don't mix it up with "lire", which means "to read".
dormir
" means "to sleep", as in "dormir huit heures". It is an irregular -ir verb.
travailler
" means "to work", as in "travailler au bureau". It is a regular -er verb.
étudier
" means "to study", as in "étudier le français". It looks like the English word "study".
jouer
" means "to play", as in "jouer au football". It is a regular -er verb.
Je veux dormir ce soir.
" means "I want to sleep tonight." The verb "dormir" (to sleep) sounds different from manger, partir and écrire.
Je veux travailler au bureau.
" means "I want to work at the office." After "je veux", the next verb stays in the infinitive: "travailler".
Je veux étudier le français.
" uses "vouloir" followed by the infinitive "étudier" (to study). "Je voudrais" is a politer way to say the same thing.
marcher
" means "to walk", as in "marcher dans le parc". It is a regular -er verb.
courir
" means "to run", as in "courir dans le parc". It is an irregular -ir verb.
nager
" means "to swim", as in "nager à la piscine". It is a regular -er verb.
cuisiner
" means "to cook" (to prepare food); "jouer" is to play, "parler" to speak and "fermer" to close.
acheter
" means to buy, as in acheter du pain (to buy bread).
J'aime nager à la piscine.
" means "I like to swim at the pool"; listen for the start of the verb: nager (to swim) has no m sound, unlike manger (to eat).
Je veux acheter du pain.
" uses the infinitive acheter (to buy) after je veux (I want), and du pain for some bread.
vendre
" means to sell, the opposite of acheter (to buy). Don't confuse it with attendre, which means to wait.
ouvrir
" means to open, as in ouvrir la porte (to open the door).
fermer
" means to close, the opposite of ouvrir (to open), as in fermer la fenêtre.
regarder
" means to look (at) or to watch, as in regarder la télé. It takes no word for at.
attendre
" means "to wait" (for example, attendre le bus); "vendre" only looks similar and means to sell.
Je veux ouvrir la porte.
" means "I want to open the door." Listen for ouvrir (open) and porte (door); the other choices change one word: fermer (close), peindre (paint) or fenêtre (window).
Je veux regarder la télé.
" means 'I want to watch TV.' Regarder takes no extra word for 'at' or 'to'.
J'attends le bus.
" uses attendre (to wait), which needs no word for 'for' in French.
aider
" means "to help"; it is a regular -er verb, as in « Je peux t'aider ? ».
aimer
" means "to love", and also "to like" for things, as in « J'aime le chocolat ».
vouloir
" means "to want" (je veux un café); "avoir besoin de" is different and means to need.
avoir besoin de
" means "to need" (j'ai besoin d'aide); "avoir envie de" means to feel like, "avoir peur de" to be afraid of and "avoir faim" to be hungry.
vivre
" means "to live" (to be alive, or to live somewhere), as in « Je vis à Paris ».
The sentence is "
Je veux aider mon ami.
" and means "I want to help my friend"; the other choices change the verb to call, listen to or invite.
Je veux aider mon ami.
" uses "vouloir" (je veux) followed by the infinitive "aider"; the friend can be mon ami, mon amie or mon copain.
le chien
" means "dog"; it is masculine, so it takes "le".
le chat
" means "cat"; it is masculine, and the final -t is silent.
l'oiseau
" means "bird"; "le" becomes "l'" before a vowel, and the word is masculine.
le cheval
" means "horse"; it is masculine, and the plural is irregular: "les chevaux".
la vache
" means "cow"; it is feminine, so it takes "la".

spans: Le chat dort sur le lit.
pieces: The sentence "
Le chat dort sur le lit.
" means the cat is sleeping on the bed; the other choices change the animal, the verb or the place.

spans: J'ai un chien et un chat
pieces: J'ai un chien et un chat
" means "I have a dog and a cat"; use "un" before masculine animal words like "chien" and "chat".
Le cheval est grand.
" uses "le" because "cheval" is masculine, and "est grand" means "is big"; "gros" also works and suggests a large, heavy animal.
le cochon
" means "pig"; it is masculine, so it takes "le".
le mouton
" means "sheep"; it is masculine, so it takes "le".
la poule
" is the live hen (feminine); chicken as meat is "le poulet".
le canard
" means "duck"; it is masculine, and the final -d is silent.
A rabbit is "
le lapin
" in French. Lapin is a masculine noun, so it takes le; le renard is a fox.

spans: Le canard est dans la rivière.
pieces: The sentence heard was "
Le canard est dans la rivière.
" It says the duck is in the river; the other choices change one word to a different animal or place.
J'ai un lapin.
" uses j'ai (I have) with un, because lapin is a masculine noun.
A mouse is "
la souris
" in French. Souris is a feminine noun, so it takes la, unlike most animals in this list.
A fish is "
le poisson
" in French. Poisson is masculine and is spelled with a double s, which gives the s sound.
A lion is "
le lion
" in French. The spelling is the same as in English, but the word is masculine and ends in a nasal vowel: the n is not pronounced as a separate sound.
A tiger is "
le tigre
" in French. Note the -re ending, where English has -er, and the masculine article le.
A bear is "
l'ours
" in French. Ours starts with a vowel, so le shortens to l'.
The speaker says "
Le chat mange du poisson.
", meaning the cat eats fish. The other choices change the animal or the food to words that sound clearly different.
Le lapin et la souris
" means the rabbit and the mouse. Remember that souris is feminine, so it takes la.
Je vois un ours.
" means I see a bear: je vois is "I see", and ours is masculine, so it takes un.
An elephant is "
l'éléphant
" in French. Éléphant starts with a vowel, so le shortens to l'. Note the two accents.
A monkey is "
le singe
" in French. Singe is a masculine noun, so it takes le.
A wolf is "
le loup
" in French. The final p is silent, and l'ours is a bear.
A fox is "
le renard
" in French. Renard is a masculine noun, and its final d is silent.
A frog is "
la grenouille
" in French. Grenouille is a feminine noun, so it takes la, and le canard is a duck.
You hear "
Le loup mange le canard.
" It means the wolf eats the duck. To tell it from the other choices, listen for the animals (loup, canard) and for the verb mange (eats).

spans: Le renard est un animal sauvage.
pieces: Le renard est un animal sauvage.
" puts the adjective "sauvage" after the noun "animal", as most French adjectives go.
A snake is "
le serpent
" in French. Serpent is a masculine noun, and its final t is silent.
"Turtle" is "
la tortue
". It is a feminine noun, so it takes "la" (une tortue).
"Bee" is "
l'abeille
". It is feminine (une abeille), and "la" shortens to "l'" before the vowel.
"Butterfly" is "
le papillon
". It is a masculine noun, so it takes "le" (un papillon).
"Spider" is "
l'araignée
". It is feminine (une araignée), and "la" becomes "l'" before the vowel.

spans: Le serpent est dans le jardin.
pieces: Le serpent est dans le jardin.

" means "The snake is in the garden." Listen for "serpent" (snake) and "jardin" (garden); the other choices swap in a different animal or place, such as "papillon" (butterfly), "tortue" (turtle) or "lit" (bed).

spans: J'ai une tortue et un papillon
pieces: J'ai une tortue et un papillon
" means I have a turtle and a butterfly. Tortue is feminine so it takes une, and papillon is masculine so it takes un.
L'araignée est grande.
" uses the feminine adjective grande because araignée is a feminine noun.
"Doctor" is "
le médecin
", the usual word for the profession. You say "docteur" mainly when you address a doctor directly.
"Nurse" is "
l'infirmier
" for a man and "l'infirmière" for a woman. "Le" becomes "l'" before the vowel.
"Teacher" as a profession is "
le professeur
", used for secondary school and university teachers. In casual speech people often shorten it to "le prof".
"Engineer" is "
l'ingénieur
". It is masculine, and "le" becomes "l'" before the vowel.
"Lawyer" is "
l'avocat
". Watch out: the same word also means "avocado".

spans: Mon frère est médecin à Paris.
pieces: The sentence "
Mon frère est médecin à Paris.
" means 'My brother is a doctor in Paris.' Listen for the profession word "médecin", which differs clearly from "dentiste" or "avocat".
Ma sœur est infirmière.
" uses the profession without an article after être, and a woman is "infirmière" with the feminine ending.
"Police officer" is "
le policier
". A female officer is "la policière".
"Firefighter" is "
le pompier
". It comes from "pompe" (pump), and firefighters work in "la caserne des pompiers" (the fire station).
le cuisinier
" is the person who cooks as a job (a woman is la cuisinière); it comes from the verb cuisiner, to cook.
"Waiter" is "
le serveur
", from the verb "servir" (to serve). A waitress is "la serveuse".
l'agriculteur
" is the person who works the land and raises crops or animals; the article elides to l' because the noun starts with a vowel.

spans: Le coiffeur travaille dans un salon.
pieces: Le coiffeur travaille dans un salon.
" pairs a job with its usual workplace: a hairdresser works in a "salon". Listen for both the job word and the place word.

spans: Je suis professeur dans une école
pieces: Je suis professeur dans une école
" means "I am a teacher in a school". In French you say your job without an article after "je suis".
Mon frère est cuisinier.
" uses "être" plus the job without an article, which is the usual way to say what someone does.
le chauffeur
" is a driver as a job, such as a taxi or bus driver (un chauffeur de taxi).
le pilote
" is the person who flies a plane; the word looks almost the same as the English "pilot".
artist →
l'artiste
. Common jobs and professions.
le musicien
" means "musician", a person who plays music; a woman is la musicienne.
l'écrivain
" means "writer", a person who writes books; "le" becomes "l'" before the vowel "é".

spans: Mon père est chauffeur de taxi.
pieces: You hear "
Mon père est chauffeur de taxi.
", meaning 'My father is a taxi driver'. Listen for "père" (not frère or oncle) and "taxi" (not bus).
Mon frère est musicien.
" uses the job directly after est without an article, which is the usual way to state someone's profession.
le scientifique
" means "scientist"; the word is the same for a man or a woman (la scientifique).
le dentiste
" means "dentist", the person who looks after your teeth (les dents); a woman is la dentiste.
le comptable
" is the person who keeps a company's accounts (un compte = an account); a woman is "la comptable".
l'électricien
" means electrician; "le" becomes "l'" because the word starts with a vowel.
le plombier
" is the person who fixes pipes and taps; it comes from "plomb" (lead), the metal old pipes were made of.
Mon père est dentiste.
" means "My father is a dentist." Listen for the job word after "est"; each job has its own distinct sound.
Je suis plombier
" means "I am a plumber." In French you say a job without "un" after "je suis".
Ma mère est comptable.
" After "est", French usually drops "un"/"une" before a job: say "est comptable", not "est une comptable".
le coiffeur
" is the person who cuts your hair (la coiffure = hairstyle); a woman is "la coiffeuse".
le journaliste
" means journalist; the word is the same for a woman, only the article changes: "la journaliste".
l'architecte
" means architect; "le" becomes "l'" before a vowel, and the word is the same for a man or a woman.
le soldat
" is a member of the army; it is a masculine noun and looks close to the English word soldier.
le secrétaire
" means secretary; for a woman you say "la secrétaire", and the spelling stays the same.

spans: Mon père est coiffeur à Paris.
pieces: The speaker says "
Mon père est coiffeur à Paris.
", meaning my father is a hairdresser in Paris; the other choices change the job, the person or the city.
Ma sœur est journaliste.
" is the simplest way to say it; after être, French usually drops the article before a profession and the word journaliste stays the same for a woman.
qui
" asks about a person (who); quel asks which, and quand asks when.
quoi
" means what at the end of a question or after a preposition, as in "Tu fais quoi ?" or "De quoi tu parles ?"; at the start of a question French uses "que" or "qu'est-ce que".
où
" asks about a place (where); the grave accent separates it from ou, which means or.
quand
" asks about time (when); où asks where, and combien asks how much or how many.
pourquoi
" asks for a reason (why); the answer often starts with parce que (because).
Comment vous vous appelez ?
" asks what someone's name is, using comment, which means how. The other choices swap in pourquoi (why), quand (when) or où (where).
Pourquoi tu pars maintenant ?
" uses pourquoi (why) to ask for a reason, in the everyday spoken style where the word order stays the same.

spans: Quand part le train, s'il vous plaît ?
pieces: Quand part le train, s'il vous plaît ?
" uses quand (when) to ask about time, and vous is used because we are speaking politely to a stranger.
comment
" asks about manner (how), as in Comment tu t'appelles ?; est-ce que only turns a sentence into a yes/no question.
combien
" asks about a quantity or price, as in "C'est combien ?" (How much is it?); "quel" means which or what.
combien de
" asks how many and is followed by a noun with no article, as in « Combien de frères as-tu ? ».
quel
" means which and agrees with its noun: quel livre, quelle heure, quels livres, quelles villes.
To ask whose something is, French says "
à qui
" (literally "to whom"), as in "À qui est ce livre ?" (Whose book is this?).
Combien de frères as-tu ?
" asks how many brothers you have; "combien de" is followed by a noun with no article.
Tu as combien de frères ?
" uses "combien de" to ask how many, followed by a noun with no article.
qu'est-ce qui
" is used when what is the subject of the verb, as in "Qu'est-ce qui se passe ?"; "qu'est-ce que" is used for the object.
qu'est-ce que
" is used when what is the object of the verb, as in "Qu'est-ce que tu veux ?"; "qu'est-ce qui" is used for the subject.
Put "
est-ce que
" in front of a statement to turn it into a yes/no question: Est-ce que tu viens ? (Are you coming?).
To ask someone's age, French uses "
quel âge
" with the verb avoir: Quel âge as-tu ? (How old are you?).
quelle heure
" asks about the time: Quelle heure est-il ? (What time is it?) or À quelle heure ... ? (At what time ...?).
Pourquoi tu pars si tôt ?
" asks why someone is leaving so early; listen for "pourquoi" (why) and "tôt" (early).
Est-ce que tu viens ?
" puts est-ce que in front of a statement to make a yes/no question.
Quel âge as-tu ?
" is how French asks someone's age, using "quel âge" with the verb avoir, not être.
où est
" asks where one thing or person is (Où est la gare ?); for several things you use où sont.
où sont
" asks where several things or people are (Où sont les clés ?); for one thing you use où est.
Où sont les enfants ?
" asks where several children are, using où sont for a plural. Listen for où (where) and for the noun enfants to tell it apart from qui (who), clés (keys) and amis (friends).

spans: Où sont les clés, s'il vous plaît ?
pieces: Où sont les clés, s'il vous plaît ?
" uses où sont because keys are plural, and vous because you are speaking politely to a receptionist.
lequel
" means "which one" for a masculine noun (Lequel préfères-tu ?); it changes to laquelle, lesquels or lesquelles to match the noun.
"which ones" is plural, so you need the plural "
lesquels
" (Lesquels préfères-tu ?); lequel means only "which one".
pourquoi pas
" means "why not" and is often used to accept a suggestion: On va au cinéma ? Pourquoi pas !
à quelle distance
" asks how far away something is: À quelle distance est la plage ? (How far is the beach?).
Où est la plage ?
" asks where the beach is; the other choices change the place to the station, the door or the post office.
Où est la gare ?
" asks where the station is; où means where.
Lequel préfères-tu ?
" uses "lequel" (which one) because it stands for "film", a masculine noun, and tu because you are speaking to a friend.
dans
" means "in" when something is inside something else: dans la maison (in the house).
sur
" means "on" when something rests on top of something else: sur la table (on the table).
sous
" means "under", for something below something else: sous le lit (under the bed).
devant
" means "in front of", as in "devant la porte". Don't confuse it with "derrière" (behind).
behind →
derrière
. Common prepositions used to locate things.

spans: Le chat est sous la table.
pieces: You hear "
Le chat est sous la table.
", meaning the cat is under the table. Listen for "sous" (under), not sur (on), devant (in front of) or derrière (behind).

spans: Le chat est sous la table.

entre

. Common prepositions used to locate things.

" means the book is near the lamp, using près de to say where something is.

spans: Le sac est sous la table.
pieces: Le sac est sous la table.
" uses sous (or en dessous de) to place the bag under the table.
far from →

. Common prepositions used to locate things.

à l'intérieur de

à l'extérieur de
. Common prepositions used to locate things.

. Common prepositions used to locate things.

spans: Le chat est devant la table.
pieces: Le chat est devant la table.
" means the cat is in front of the table. Listen for "devant", which sounds clearly different from "derrière" (behind), "sur" (on) and "sous" (under).

spans: Le parc est loin de l'école.
pieces: "loin de" means far from, so the park is placed far from the school: "
Le parc est loin de l'école.
against →
contre
. Common prepositions used to locate things.
à travers
" means "through", going from one side to the other, as in à travers la forêt (through the forest).
le long de
" means "along", following the length of something, as in le long de la rivière (along the river). "de" becomes "du" before a masculine noun: le long du mur.
"among" is "
parmi
", used for one thing in a group of several: "parmi les livres" (among the books).
vers
" means "towards", showing direction, as in Il marche vers la gare (He walks towards the station).

spans: Le chat est contre le mur.
pieces: Le chat est contre le mur.
" uses "contre" for "against", meaning touching the wall. "Sous", "devant" and "près de" place the cat elsewhere.

spans: Il marche le long de la rivière.
pieces: Il marche le long de la rivière.
" means He walks along the river; "le long de" means "along".

spans: Le chat marche le long du mur.
pieces: Le chat marche le long du mur.
" uses "le long de" (along), and "de" + "le" becomes "du" before the masculine noun "mur".
chez
" means at someone's place and goes before a person or pronoun: "chez moi", "chez Marie".
de
" means "from", as in Je viens de Paris (I come from Paris). It combines with le and les: du, des.
à

ici

il est minuit
" means it's midnight (12 a.m.); "midi" is noon.

" means "quarter to four": French takes the next hour and subtracts a quarter. Trois heures et quart is quarter past three.

spans: Il est six heures du matin.

spans: Je voudrais un thé avec du sucre
pieces: This is a polite way to order a drink and add sugar: "
Je voudrais un thé avec du sucre
" means I would like a tea with sugar.

spans: Je voudrais une douzaine d'œufs, s'il vous plaît.
pieces: Je voudrais une douzaine d'œufs, s'il vous plaît.
" uses je voudrais and vous to ask a shop assistant politely, and "une douzaine de" means a dozen (de becomes d' before œufs).
Salt is "
le sel
" in French. It is a masculine noun, so it takes "le".
Meat is "
la viande
" in French. It is a feminine noun, so it takes "la".
Chicken, as a dish or as the bird, is "
le poulet
" in French. It is masculine, so it takes "le".
Fish, both the food and the animal, is "
le poisson
" in French. It is masculine, so it takes "le".
Vegetable is "
le légume
" in French. It is masculine even though it ends in -e.

spans: Je voudrais du poulet et des légumes.
pieces: The speaker says "
Je voudrais du poulet et des légumes.
", meaning I would like some chicken and some vegetables. Each wrong choice swaps one food word for a clearly different one.

spans: Je voudrais du poisson et du pain.
pieces: Je voudrais du poisson et du pain.
" uses "je voudrais" (I would like) to order politely, with "du" before masculine foods.
Fruit is "
le fruit
" in French. It has the same spelling as in English and is masculine.
Apple is "
la pomme
" in French. It is a feminine noun, so it takes "la".
Orange (the fruit) is "
l'orange
" in French. The noun is feminine and starts with a vowel, so "la" becomes "l'".
Banana is "
la banane
" in French. It is a feminine noun, so it takes "la".
Potato is "
la pomme de terre
" in French, literally "apple of the earth". It is feminine, like "pomme".

spans: Je voudrais du poisson et de la soupe.
pieces: The speaker orders fish and soup: "
Je voudrais du poisson et de la soupe.
" The other choices change one food word to a different food.

spans: Je voudrais une pomme et une banane
pieces: Je voudrais une pomme et une banane
" is a polite way to ask for two fruits. Both nouns are feminine, so each takes "une".

spans: Je voudrais un café et un gâteau, s'il vous plaît.
pieces: Je voudrais un café et un gâteau, s'il vous plaît.
" uses "je voudrais" for a polite order, and both "café" and "gâteau" are masculine, so they take "un".
le riz
" is the French word for rice; riz is a masculine noun, so it takes le.
la soupe
" is the French word for soup; soupe is a feminine noun, so it takes la.
"Cake" is "
le gâteau
". Note the accent on the â and the plural with -x: des gâteaux.
"Juice" is "
le jus
", with a silent s, as in un jus d'orange (an orange juice).
"Breakfast", the morning meal, is "
le petit-déjeuner
". Literally it means a "small lunch" (déjeuner = lunch).

spans: Je voudrais du riz et du poulet.
pieces: The speaker says "
Je voudrais du riz et du poulet.
", meaning 'I would like some rice and some chicken'. The wrong choices change one food word (poisson, lait, sel).

spans: Je voudrais un jus et un gâteau.
pieces: Je voudrais un jus et un gâteau.
" uses "je voudrais", the polite way to order, and "un" because "jus" and "gâteau" are masculine.

spans: Allez tout droit, puis tournez à gauche après la banque.
pieces: The speaker says "
Allez tout droit, puis tournez à gauche après la banque.
" This means go straight ahead, then turn left after the bank.

spans: Le café est en face de la poste
pieces: Le café est en face de la poste
" uses "en face de" to say the café is opposite the post office.
L'hôtel est tout près d'ici.
" uses "tout près" for very close, where "tout" strengthens "près", and "d'ici" means from here. Saying "juste à côté" (right next door) is another natural way to say it.

spans: Le musée est derrière l'église, près d'ici.
pieces: The speaker says "
Le musée est derrière l'église, près d'ici.
", meaning the museum is behind the church and close to here. Listen for derrière (behind) versus devant (in front of), près (near) versus loin (far), and église versus avenue.

spans: La pharmacie est à côté de l'arrêt de bus.
pieces: La pharmacie est à côté de l'arrêt de bus.
" uses "à côté de" for next to, followed by "l'arrêt de bus" for the bus stop.

spans: Prenez la rue à droite après le pont.
pieces: The speaker says "
Prenez la rue à droite après le pont.
" Listen carefully: "rue" has the French u sound and no final t, while "route" has an ou sound and ends in t; the other choices change "pont" to "feu" or "droite" to "gauche".
Tournez à gauche au carrefour
" is a typical direction meaning turn left at the crossroads. You use the vous command form "tournez", and "au" joins à and le before "carrefour".
Allez tout droit jusqu'au feu.
" uses the polite vous command form, with "tout droit" for straight ahead and "jusqu'au" for as far as.

spans: Le magasin est juste au coin de la rue.
pieces: Le magasin est juste au coin de la rue.
" means the shop is right at the corner of the street; the other choices change one word: musée instead of magasin, bout instead of coin, or place instead of rue.

spans: Prenez la deuxième sortie au rond-point.
pieces: Prenez la deuxième sortie au rond-point.
" uses "prenez", the polite vous command of prendre, with "la deuxième sortie" for the second exit and "au rond-point" for at the roundabout.

spans: Je cherche la gare dans ce quartier.
pieces: The speaker says "
Je cherche la gare dans ce quartier.
", meaning they are looking for the station in this neighbourhood; the other choices change the place, the area or the verb.

spans: Je suis perdu dans ce quartier
pieces: Je suis perdu dans ce quartier
" means "I am lost in this neighborhood." Here "perdu" works as an adjective meaning lost, and "quartier" is a masculine noun, which is why it goes with "ce."
J'habite dans un quartier calme.
" uses "quartier" (masculine, so "un") with the adjective "calme" to describe a quiet neighbourhood.

spans: Il pleut beaucoup en automne dans cette région.
pieces: The speaker says "
Il pleut beaucoup en automne dans cette région.
", meaning it rains a lot in autumn in this region; the other choices change the weather, the season or the place.

spans: Il fait très froid en hiver.
pieces: French uses "il fait" plus an adjective for the weather, and winter takes "en", so "
Il fait très froid en hiver.
" is the natural way to say it.

spans: Demain il y aura du soleil le matin.
pieces: You hear "
Demain il y aura du soleil le matin.
", which says there will be sun tomorrow morning. Listen for the weather noun: soleil, brouillard, verglas and tonnerre sound clearly different.

spans: Il fait un temps magnifique aujourd'hui
pieces: Il fait un temps magnifique aujourd'hui
" means the weather is wonderful today. French uses "il fait" with "temps" to describe the weather.

spans: Il y a beaucoup de vent ce matin.
pieces: Il y a beaucoup de vent ce matin.
" uses "il y a" with "beaucoup de" and a noun to describe the weather, just like "il y a du vent".

spans: Demain, il va pleuvoir et il fera froid.
pieces: The sentence heard is "
Demain, il va pleuvoir et il fera froid.
" and it means tomorrow it will rain and be cold. The other choices change one word: neiger (snow), chaud (hot) or frais (cool).

spans: Hier, il a fait un temps épouvantable et il a plu toute la journée.
pieces: Hier, il a fait un temps épouvantable et il a plu toute la journée.
" uses "il fait un temps …" for the weather, put in the past with "il a fait", and "il a plu" (from pleuvoir) for the rain.

spans: Demain, il va pleuvoir toute la journée.
pieces: The speaker says "
Demain, il va pleuvoir toute la journée.
", a forecast for rain tomorrow using aller + infinitive for the near future.

spans: Il y a beaucoup de vent ce matin
pieces: Il y a beaucoup de vent ce matin
" is a natural way to say it is very windy this morning, using il y a to describe the weather.

spans: Hier soir, il y a eu un gros orage avec beaucoup de pluie.
pieces: Hier soir, il y a eu un gros orage avec beaucoup de pluie.
" uses il y a eu, the past of il y a, to describe a storm that happened last night.

spans: Hier, il a plu toute la journée.
pieces: The sentence "
Hier, il a plu toute la journée.
" means it rained all day yesterday; the other choices use verbs that sound different and say it froze, slept or ate.

spans: En hiver, il fait souvent froid et le ciel est couvert de nuages.
pieces: French describes the weather with "il fait" plus an adjective, and a cloudy sky is "couvert de nuages". So you say "
En hiver, il fait souvent froid et le ciel est couvert de nuages.
Grand means big or tall, so its opposite is "
petit
", meaning small or short.
Chaud means hot, so its opposite is "
froid
", meaning cold.
Rapide means fast, so its opposite is "
lent
", meaning slow (feminine: lente).
Facile means easy, so its opposite is "
difficile
", meaning difficult. It has the same form for masculine and feminine.
Propre means clean, so its opposite is "
sale
", meaning dirty.

spans: Aujourd'hui, la soupe est trop chaude pour moi.
pieces: You hear "
Aujourd'hui, la soupe est trop chaude pour moi.
", meaning the soup is too hot for me. Listen for "chaude" (hot), not "froide" (cold), "salée" (salty) or "sucrée" (sweet).

spans: Ma valise est lourde mais mon sac est léger
pieces: Ma valise est lourde mais mon sac est léger
" pairs opposites: "lourde" (heavy) and "léger" (light). "Lourde" is feminine to match "valise".

spans: La soupe est chaude mais l'eau est froide.
pieces: Chaud and froid are opposites, and both take a feminine ending to agree with "la soupe" and "l'eau", so you write "
La soupe est chaude mais l'eau est froide.
Plein means full, so its opposite is "
vide
", meaning empty, as in un verre vide (an empty glass).
Riche means rich, so its opposite is "
pauvre
", meaning poor.
vieux
" (old) is the opposite of "jeune" (young); its feminine is "vieille", and it becomes "vieil" before a masculine noun starting with a vowel.
faible
" (weak) is the opposite of "fort" (strong): they describe opposite levels of strength.
triste
" (sad) is the opposite of "heureux" (happy): they describe opposite feelings.

spans: Mon grand-père est vieux, mais il est très fort.
pieces: The speaker says "
Mon grand-père est vieux, mais il est très fort.
" meaning my grandfather is old but very strong; the other choices swap one adjective for a clearly different one.

spans: Le verre est vide et la bouteille est pleine.
pieces: Le verre est vide et la bouteille est pleine.
" uses the opposites vide (empty) and plein (full), and pleine takes the feminine form to agree with la bouteille.
laid
" (ugly) is the opposite of "beau" (beautiful): they describe opposite appearances.
fermé
" (closed) is the opposite of "ouvert" (open): a door or a shop is either one or the other.
bas
" (low) is the opposite of "haut" (high): they describe opposite heights.
court
" (short) is the opposite of "long" (long): they describe opposite lengths.
bon marché
" (cheap) is the opposite of "cher" (expensive), and it never changes form: une robe bon marché.

spans: Cette valise est lourde, mais mon sac est léger.
pieces: Cette valise est lourde, mais mon sac est léger.
" "Mais" signals a contrast, here between "lourde" (heavy) and "léger" (light).

spans: La porte est ouverte, mais la fenêtre est fermée
pieces: La porte est ouverte, mais la fenêtre est fermée
" sets two opposites side by side, ouvert (open) and fermé (closed), and each adjective takes an extra -e because porte and fenêtre are feminine.
Le magasin est fermé aujourd'hui.
" uses "fermé" (closed), the opposite of "ouvert" (open), and the adjective stays masculine because "magasin" is masculine.
léger
" (light) is the opposite of "lourd" (heavy): they describe opposite weights.
mou
" (soft) is the opposite of "dur" (hard): they describe opposite textures, like a hard bed versus a soft one.
For colours, "
foncé
" (dark) is the opposite of "clair" (light), as in bleu clair versus bleu foncé.
bruyant
" (noisy) is the opposite of "calme" (quiet, calm): they describe opposite levels of noise, as in une rue calme versus une rue bruyante.
méchant
" (mean, nasty) is the opposite of "gentil" (kind): they describe opposite ways of treating people.

spans: Cette valise est trop lourde pour moi.
pieces: Cette valise est trop lourde pour moi.
" "Trop" means "too" before an adjective, and "lourde" (heavy) agrees with feminine "valise".

spans: La rue est calme mais les voisins sont bruyants.
pieces: La rue est calme mais les voisins sont bruyants.
" pairs the opposites "calme" and "bruyants", and the adjective "bruyants" takes the plural to agree with "les voisins".
impoli
" (rude) is the opposite of "poli" (polite): French often forms opposites with the prefix im- or in-.
Describing a person, "
mince
" (slim) is the opposite of "gros" (fat, big).
mouillé
" (wet) is the opposite of "sec" (dry), as in "une serviette mouillée" (a wet towel).
tard
" (late) is the opposite of "tôt" (early); both are adverbs, so they never change form, as in "Je me couche tard."
For objects, "
usé
" (worn out) is the opposite of "neuf" (brand new), as in des chaussures neuves versus des chaussures usées.

spans: Ma serviette est mouillée, mais la tienne est sèche.
pieces: The speaker says "
Ma serviette est mouillée, mais la tienne est sèche.
" (My towel is wet, but yours is dry), using the opposites mouillé and sec.

spans: Je me couche tard le samedi
pieces: Je me couche tard le samedi
" means 'I go to bed late on Saturdays'; tard (late) is the opposite of tôt (early).

spans: Mes chaussures neuves sont très chères, mais les vieilles sont usées.
pieces: Mes chaussures neuves sont très chères, mais les vieilles sont usées.
" contrasts neuves (new) with vieilles (old), and usées (worn out) describes the old pair; all the adjectives agree with the feminine plural chaussures.

spans: Le matin, je me lève à sept heures.
pieces: The speaker says "
Le matin, je me lève à sept heures.
" meaning they get up at seven in the morning; the other choices change the time of day, the verb or the hour.

spans: Je me couche tard le soir.
pieces: The reflexive verb "se coucher" with "je" becomes "
Je me couche tard le soir.
", and the time phrase can come first or last.

spans: Hier soir, je me suis couché très tard.
pieces: The speaker says "
Hier soir, je me suis couché très tard.
", meaning he went to bed very late last night; the other choices change one word (levé, vite, matin).

spans: Je me douche avant le travail
pieces: Je me douche avant le travail
" means "I take a shower before work": the reflexive verb se doucher takes the pronoun "me" to match the subject "je".

spans: Je me lave et je m'habille avant le petit déjeuner.
pieces: With "je" the reflexive pronoun elides before a vowel, so you write "
Je me lave et je m'habille avant le petit déjeuner.

spans: Le matin, je me lave et je m'habille vite.
pieces: You hear "
Le matin, je me lave et je m'habille vite.
" It describes a morning routine: washing and getting dressed quickly. Listen for matin (morning) versus soir (evening), and for vite (quickly) versus tard (late).

spans: Je me prépare vite et ensuite je pars au travail.
pieces: Je me prépare vite et ensuite je pars au travail.
" uses the reflexive verb se préparer with me, and a connector like ensuite or puis links the two actions.

spans: Demain matin, je vais me lever très tôt.
pieces: You hear "
Demain matin, je vais me lever très tôt.
", meaning 'Tomorrow morning, I am going to get up very early.' Listen for lever (get up), not coucher (go to bed) or laver (wash), and for tôt (early) versus tard (late).

spans: Nous nous occupons de la maison
pieces: Nous nous occupons de la maison
" means 'We take care of the house.' With nous, the reflexive pronoun is also nous and the verb ends in -ons.

spans: Je me prépare vite avant de sortir.
pieces: Je me prépare vite avant de sortir.
" uses the reflexive verb se préparer with me, followed by avant de and an infinitive.

spans: Le dimanche, je me lève très tard.
pieces: The speaker says "
Le dimanche, je me lève très tard.
", meaning they get up very late on Sundays. The other choices change the verb, the day or tard/tôt.

spans: Je ne m'inquiète pas, je me détends ce soir.
pieces: With the subject "je" both reflexive verbs take me/m' and the first-person form, and ne … pas goes around the first verb: "
Je ne m'inquiète pas, je me détends ce soir.
The speaker says "
Nous allons voyager demain matin.
" using aller in the near future with the infinitive "voyager"; the other choices change the verb to manger, partir or étudier.

spans: Ce soir, je vais manger avec mes amis.
pieces: Ce soir, je vais manger avec mes amis.
" uses "je vais" plus an infinitive to say what you are going to do soon.

spans: Mon ami va arriver tard ce soir.
pieces: Mon ami va arriver tard ce soir.
" uses the singular subject with "va" followed by the infinitive "arriver" to express the near future.

spans: Demain, nous allons visiter le musée.
pieces: The speaker says "
Demain, nous allons visiter le musée.
", using nous allons plus the infinitive to talk about a plan for tomorrow.

spans: Je vais téléphoner à ma mère ce soir.
pieces: The near future is formed with aller and an infinitive, so "
Je vais téléphoner à ma mère ce soir.
" says what you are about to do.

spans: Nous allons manger au restaurant demain soir.
pieces: The sentence "
Nous allons manger au restaurant demain soir.
" uses the near future: allons plus the infinitive manger, for a plan tomorrow evening.

spans: Je vais appeler ma sœur ce soir
pieces: Je vais appeler ma sœur ce soir
" uses vais plus the infinitive appeler to say what you are about to do.

spans: Tu vas prendre le train demain.
pieces: Tu vas prendre le train demain.
" uses "vas" (the tu form of aller) followed by the infinitive "prendre" to say what you are going to do soon.

spans: Demain, nous allons manger chez mes parents.
pieces: Demain, nous allons manger chez mes parents.
" uses aller + infinitive ("allons manger") for a near-future plan, and "demain" marks it as tomorrow.

spans: Nous allons dîner au restaurant ce soir.
pieces: The near future is built with aller plus an infinitive, so "
Nous allons dîner au restaurant ce soir.
" uses "allons" with "dîner"; "on va" is the everyday spoken alternative.

spans: Demain, nous allons voyager en train.
pieces: The sentence "
Demain, nous allons voyager en train.
" uses aller with the infinitive voyager to say what we are going to do tomorrow.
Je vais apprendre le français
" uses vais with the infinitive apprendre to say what you are going to do.

spans: Tu vas répondre au message ce soir.
pieces: Tu vas répondre au message ce soir.
" combines tu vas (aller for tu) with the infinitive répondre to express the near future.

spans: Demain, je vais aller chez le médecin avec ma mère.
pieces: Demain, je vais aller chez le médecin avec ma mère.
" Listen for "médecin" (doctor, not dentiste) and "ma mère" (mother, not père or sœur).

spans: J'ai mal à la gorge depuis hier.
pieces: J'ai mal à la gorge depuis hier.
" uses avoir mal à + body part, and "gorge" is feminine so it takes "à la"; "depuis" shows the pain started yesterday and continues.

spans: Le docteur m'a donné un sirop pour la toux.
pieces: The speaker says "
Le docteur m'a donné un sirop pour la toux.
", meaning the doctor gave me a cough syrup; the wrong choices change only the last word to a different body part or illness.

spans: J'ai mal à la gorge depuis hier
pieces: J'ai mal à la gorge depuis hier
" means 'I have had a sore throat since yesterday', using avoir mal à la plus a feminine body part.
J'ai très mal au dos.
" uses avoir mal à plus the masculine noun dos, which contracts to au, and très adds 'a lot'.

spans: Le médecin m'a donné une ordonnance pour demain.
pieces: The sentence heard was "
Le médecin m'a donné une ordonnance pour demain.
" meaning the doctor gave me a prescription for tomorrow; the other choices change the day, the professional or the item.

spans: J'ai mal au dos et je dois voir le médecin.
pieces: J'ai mal au dos et je dois voir le médecin.
" uses "avoir mal à" for pain, with "au" because "dos" is masculine, and "devoir" to express need.

spans: Le médecin m'a donné une ordonnance ce matin.
pieces: The sentence is "
Le médecin m'a donné une ordonnance ce matin.
" and means the doctor gave me a prescription this morning; the other choices change the noun to a shot, a lozenge or an X-ray.

spans: J'ai de la fièvre depuis hier
pieces: J'ai de la fièvre depuis hier
" means 'I have had a fever since yesterday'; you use "avoir de la fièvre" for a fever and "depuis" for how long it has lasted.

spans: Je dois voir un spécialiste après l'opération.
pieces: Je dois voir un spécialiste après l'opération.
" uses "dois" (from devoir, must) followed by the infinitive "voir", and "après l'opération" says when; "J'ai besoin de voir" is also correct.

spans: Le médecin m'a donné une ordonnance pour ma toux.
pieces: The doctor gave the speaker a prescription for a cough, so the sentence is "
Le médecin m'a donné une ordonnance pour ma toux.
" The other choices change the medicine, the body part or the person.

spans: J'ai mal au genou et je dois voir le médecin.
pieces: J'ai mal au genou et je dois voir le médecin.
" uses avoir mal à for a pain and devoir plus an infinitive for something you must do.

spans: Je voudrais essayer cette robe en taille moyenne.
pieces: The speaker says "
Je voudrais essayer cette robe en taille moyenne.
", asking to try on a dress in a medium size; the other choices change the verb, the garment or the size.

spans: Où est la cabine d'essayage, s'il vous plaît ?
pieces: Où est la cabine d'essayage, s'il vous plaît ?
" is a polite way to ask where the fitting room is, using vous as with a shop assistant.

spans: Cette jupe est trop petite pour moi.
pieces: Cette jupe est trop petite pour moi.
" uses the feminine form "petite" because "jupe" is feminine, and "trop" means too.

spans: Je voudrais essayer cette veste dans la cabine.
pieces: The sentence is "
Je voudrais essayer cette veste dans la cabine.
" and it means 'I would like to try on this jacket in the fitting room.' The other choices change the verb, the garment or the place.

spans: Cette veste est trop grande pour moi.
pieces: Cette veste est trop grande pour moi.
" uses "trop" before the adjective, which agrees with the feminine noun "veste" as "grande".

spans: Je voudrais essayer ce pantalon noir, s'il vous plaît.
pieces: The sentence is "
Je voudrais essayer ce pantalon noir, s'il vous plaît.
" and it means you would like to try on these black trousers; the other choices change the item, the colour or the verb.

spans: Cette jupe me va très bien
pieces: Cette jupe me va très bien
" means this skirt fits or suits me very well, using the idiom "aller bien".

spans: Je voudrais essayer cette chemise blanche, s'il vous plaît.
pieces: Je voudrais essayer cette chemise blanche, s'il vous plaît.
" uses the polite "je voudrais" plus the infinitive "essayer", and "blanche" is feminine to agree with "chemise".

spans: Je voudrais essayer cette robe dans une autre taille.
pieces: The speaker says "
Je voudrais essayer cette robe dans une autre taille.
", asking to try the dress on in a different size. The other sentences change the verb, the garment or the size/colour, which all sound different.

spans: Où sont les cabines d'essayage, s'il vous plaît ?
pieces: Où sont les cabines d'essayage, s'il vous plaît ?
" uses "où sont" (where are) with the plural noun "cabines d'essayage" (fitting rooms), and vous is the polite form for a shop assistant.

spans: Je voudrais essayer ce pantalon dans la cabine.
pieces: The sentence is "
Je voudrais essayer ce pantalon dans la cabine.
" It means you would like to try the trousers on in the fitting room; the other choices change one word you can clearly hear (rue, acheter, manteau).

spans: Avez-vous quelque chose de plus petit ?
pieces: You say "
Avez-vous quelque chose de plus petit ?
" to ask a shop assistant for a smaller size; the adjective stays masculine singular after "quelque chose de".

spans: Cette chemise est trop grande pour moi, où est la cabine d'essayage ?
pieces: Cette chemise est trop grande pour moi, où est la cabine d'essayage ?
" uses "trop" for 'too' and the feminine "grande" because "chemise" is feminine.

spans: On se retrouve devant le cinéma à huit heures.
pieces: The speaker suggests meeting in front of the cinema at eight: "
On se retrouve devant le cinéma à huit heures.
" The other choices change the place, the time or "devant" (in front of).

spans: Tu es libre samedi pour dîner chez moi ?
pieces: A friendly invitation can be a question about availability or a direct offer: "
Tu es libre samedi pour dîner chez moi ?
" uses "tu" with "chez moi" (at my place).

spans: On se retrouve devant la gare à huit heures.
pieces: The speaker says "
On se retrouve devant la gare à huit heures.
", meaning they will meet in front of the station at eight o'clock.

spans: Je voudrais te voir demain soir

"; "la piscine" is a swimming pool and "la patinoire" is an ice rink.

", meaning our team won the match last night; "perdu" would mean lost and "demain" would mean tomorrow.

pieces: The reflexive verb s'entraîner gives "

"; "le lundi" or "tous les lundis" both express a habit on Mondays.
le bureau

la réunion

pieces: Mon patron est dans le bureau avec un collègue.

spans: J'ai une réunion avec mon patron

spans: Mon collègue est dans le bureau.
pieces: Mon collègue est dans le bureau.

le salaire

l'horaire
" is your schedule, the hours you work; "le bureau" is the office.
la date limite
" is the deadline, literally the 'limit date' by which the work must be finished.
le projet

le courriel
" is the official French word for an email; in everyday speech in France people often say "le mail".

spans: Je dois envoyer ce courriel au client demain.
pieces: Je dois envoyer ce courriel au client demain.

le rapport
" is a written report, as in « Je dois finir le rapport ce soir ». "le courriel" is an email, not a report.
le contrat
" is a contract. Note the spelling: there is no c before the t, unlike English contract.
l'entretien

la promotion

spans: Demain, j'ai un entretien avec le patron.

Demain, j'ai un entretien avec le patron.

pieces: Je dois finir le rapport ce soir

spans: J'ai envoyé mon CV à l'entreprise hier.

la tâche

le client

spans: Je travaille avec une bonne équipe au bureau.

spans: Je pars en vacances en août.
pieces: Je pars en vacances en août.

la présentation

l'ordinateur

pieces: Target phrase: "

" Starting with "Est-ce que" turns a statement into a yes/no question, and "tu" fits asking a friend.
Target phrase: "
On peut se voir demain ?
" In everyday speech "on" means "we", and a rising voice alone makes it a question.
Target phrase: "
Je dois partir maintenant.
" "Devoir" plus an infinitive means "to have to", and the final "s" of "dois" and "t" of "maintenant" are silent.
Target phrase: "
Pouvez-vous m'aider, s'il vous plaît ?
" Inverting "vous pouvez" to "Pouvez-vous" gives a polite question for asking a stranger for help.
Target phrase: "
Je cherche la gare.
" "Chercher" means "to look for" and takes no preposition, so there is no word for "for" before "la gare".
Target phrase: "
C'est à quelle distance ?
" This is a natural spoken way to ask how far away something is, with "à" before "quelle distance".
Target phrase: "
Combien ça coûte ?
" This is the everyday way to ask a price, and the final "-te" of "coûte" is pronounced.
Target phrase: "
Je voudrais réserver une table.
" "Je voudrais" (I would like) is the polite form to use when booking at a restaurant.
Target phrase: "
Avez-vous une chambre libre ?
" Inverting to "Avez-vous" makes a polite question for a hotel receptionist, and "libre" means available.

pieces: Target phrase: "

" In spoken French "à quelle heure" can come at the end of the question, with the voice rising.
Target phrase: "

" "Avoir besoin de" means "to need", and "de" shortens to "d'" before "un".

spans: Je ne me sens pas bien.
pieces: Je ne me sens pas bien.
" means "I don't feel well." The reflexive "me" sits between "ne" and the verb, and the final "s" of "sens" is silent.

spans: Qu'est-ce que tu fais ce week-end ?
pieces: Qu'est-ce que tu fais ce week-end ?
" means "What are you doing this weekend?" "Qu'est-ce que" is said quickly, like "kess-kuh", and "tu" suits a friend.
Je travaille dans un bureau.
" means "I work in an office." In "travaille" the "ill" sounds like the English "y" and the final "e" is silent.

spans: J'étudie le français depuis deux ans.
pieces: J'étudie le français depuis deux ans.
" means "I've been studying French for two years." French uses the present tense with "depuis" for something still going on, and "deux ans" is linked with a "z" sound.
Nous habitons ici depuis longtemps.
" means "We have lived here for a long time." The present tense goes with "depuis", and "nous habitons" is linked with a "z" sound.
Elle arrive dans dix minutes.
" means "She's arriving in ten minutes." "Dans" plus a time means "in ... from now", and "dix" before "minutes" is said "dee".
Il est parti hier soir.
" means "He left last night." "Partir" takes "être" in the past tense, so you say "est parti", and the final "t" of "parti" is not pronounced.

spans: Je vais chez le médecin demain.
pieces: Je vais chez le médecin demain.
" means "I'm going to the doctor's tomorrow." Use "chez" when you go to a person's place, such as a doctor or a friend.
Tu peux venir avec nous ?
" means "Can you come with us?" A rising voice at the end turns the sentence into a question, and "tu" suits a friend.
C'est une bonne idée.
" means "That's a good idea." "Idée" is feminine, so it takes "une" and "bonne".
Je suis d'accord avec toi.
" means "I agree with you." French uses "être d'accord" (to be in agreement), and "toi" is the form used after "avec".
Je ne suis pas d'accord.
" means "I don't agree." The negation "ne ... pas" goes around the verb "suis".
